summary: Defines two strategies for folding long lines in width-bounded text such as Internet-Drafts and RFCs: a single backslash strategy and a double backslash strategy. These let examples be wrapped and later restored.

eli5.summary: When a sentence is too long for the page, you break it and mark where. This explains how to mark so the original can be rebuilt.

subtitle: Two strategies for wrapping long lines in plain-text RFCs and drafts, and unwrapping them automatically.

tldr.problem: RFCs and Internet-Drafts must have lines of 72 characters or fewer, but examples, code, and generated content often exceed this limit. There has been no standard convention for marking where lines were folded, making it hard to automatically unfold and validate the original content.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two backslash-based strategies. The single backslash strategy marks folded lines with a backslash, and the double backslash strategy uses two backslashes to mark both the fold and its continuation point. Both include a self-describing header so tools can detect and reverse the folding.
tldr.outcome: Authors and tools can now fold long lines consistently and tools can automatically restore the original content for validation. YANG modules and other structured code extracted from documents can be validated as originally written.

facts.label: Folding marker
facts.value: Backslash character at end of line

today: RFC 8792 is an Informational document standardizing text folding for RFCs and Internet-Drafts. It is used by the RFC Editor's xml2rfc tooling and by authors who need to include long-line content such as code examples in documents.

sections.title: The Line-Length Problem
sections.content:
RFC 7994 requires that every line in an RFC or Internet-Draft be limited to 72 characters followed by a newline. However, many RFCs include examples of code, configuration files, or other structured content that naturally has lines longer than 72 characters. The xml2rfc tool, widely used to generate RFCs, does not automatically wrap such content; it issues a warning and leaves the long line as-is.

Historically, there was no RFC Editor convention for how to handle this. Authors marked folded lines differently or not at all. This made it impossible for tools to automatically reconstitute the original content for validation. For example, a YANG module extracted from an Internet-Draft should be valid as originally written, but folded lines prevented validation.

This RFC defines two standard strategies for folding long lines so that tools can fold them automatically during document generation and unfold them automatically when extracting content for validation.
sections.eli5: Documents have a rule: no line longer than 72 characters. But code examples are often longer. Before, nobody had a standard way to mark where a line was broken, so tools could not fix it back.

sections.title: The Two Folding Strategies
sections.content:
The RFC defines two closely related strategies that differ in how they mark continuation.

Single Backslash Strategy: A line ending with a backslash character indicates that the next line is a continuation. The continuation begins at the first non-space character on the next line. This strategy is more readable because it does not introduce extra markers into the content. However, it cannot handle cases where the next line would need to start with a space character, because the algorithm skips leading spaces.

Double Backslash Strategy: A line ending with a backslash is followed by a continuation line that starts with a backslash (after any leading spaces). The actual continuation content follows the second backslash. This strategy is more robust: any character, including spaces, can begin the continuation. However, the extra backslash markers make the folded output less readable.

The RFC recommends that implementations first try the single backslash strategy and fall back to double backslash only when single backslash cannot fold the input (for example, when a line contains only spaces or must continue with a space character). Both strategies use a self-describing header so tools can detect which strategy was used.
sections.eli5: With single backslash, you mark where the break is and the next line picks up where you left off. With double backslash, you mark the break and also mark where the next part starts, so you can handle tricky cases like lines that start with a space.

sections.title: Header and Folding Examples
sections.content:
Both strategies start with a two-line header. For single backslash, the header line contains the text NOTE: '\' line wrapping per RFC 8792 (36 characters), and the second line is blank. For double backslash, it contains NOTE: '\\' line wrapping per RFC 8792 (37 characters), also followed by a blank line.

When a line exceeds the desired maximum (default 69 characters), the folding algorithm determines a safe fold point before the maximum, inserts a backslash at that position followed by a newline, and continues the content on the next line (with optional leading spaces for readability, in the double backslash case with a leading backslash). A very long line may be folded multiple times. The default maximum line length is 69 characters, chosen to fit the RFC page width of 72 characters including the newline.

Unfolding reverses the process: tools scan for the header, remove it, and for each folded line, remove the backslash(es) and the newline, bringing the next line up. If a line was folded multiple times, each fold is removed in turn.
sections.eli5: The header is like a note that says 'I folded some lines here using method X.' Then when you see a backslash at the end of a line, you know the next line continues it.

sections.title: When and How to Use
sections.content:
These strategies are primarily for structured text content such as source code (XML, JSON, ABNF, YANG) or other line-oriented formats. They are NOT recommended for graphical artwork or ASCII diagrams, because folding disrupts the visual layout. Many formats also have better built-in options: YANG has string concatenation with the + operator, and tools like pyang have options to limit line length.

The RFC recommends that authors first use format-specific line-length controls when available, and only fall back to these folding strategies when necessary. The xml2rfc tool can apply folding during document generation. A self-describing header enables tools to unfold automatically when extracting and validating content. The RFC includes a Bash script (rfcfold) that demonstrates how to fold and unfold text content.
sections.eli5: Use this method when you have code or structured text that is too long and it cannot be shortened using the tool's own features. The header makes it clear that folding happened, so the computer can reverse it.
